Description: Five years after the Great Fire of 1845 burned a third of Pittsburgh, the rebuilt brick city of 46,000 smokes with glassworks, rolling mills, foundries and boatyards. Choose your industry and where to found your works.
Irish refugees from the Great Famine and Germans fleeing the failed revolutions of 1848 arrive by canal and river, settling in the Point, Lawrenceville and Allegheny City.
Congress passes the Fugitive Slave Act. Pittsburgh's Black community meets in protest, Martin Delany vows resistance, and hundreds flee to Canada within weeks.
McKeesport, a coal-mining village since 1830, gets its first iron and steel mill.
The first railroad reaches Allegheny City from the west, beginning the end of the canal era.
Bernard Lauth and B.F. Jones found the American Iron Company on the Monongahela south of the city: the seed of Jones & Laughlin.
The Pennsylvania Railroad opens its line over the mountains. Philadelphia is now hours, not days, away; the canal and the Conestoga wagon fade.
The city's first chartered public hospital opens a four-story, 120-patient building in the 12th Ward.
Cholera sweeps the crowded riverfront wards. Hundreds die; families flee to the hills.
Banker James Laughlin buys out Lauth's share of the American Iron Company. Its American Mine opens to feed the furnaces with coal.
Twice burned out, Western University finishes a 16-room brick building at Ross and Diamond Streets. Classes resume the next year.
Pittsburgh opens Central High School, one of the region's first public high schools.
Anti-slavery delegates meet in Pittsburgh, form the first Republican National Committee, and call the convention that will nominate Frémont.
Pennsylvania sells its canal and portage railroad to the Pennsylvania Railroad for $7.5 million. Within a year the Philadelphia route is all-rail.
A financial panic spreads from New York. Iron prices collapse and mills bank their furnaces.
Iron puddlers found the Sons of Vulcan at a Diamond Street hotel bar, with Miles Humphreys as Grand Master. It becomes one of the era's strongest unions.
Edwin Drake strikes oil up the Allegheny. Refineries spring up along Pittsburgh's riverbanks and barges of crude crowd the wharves.
President-elect Lincoln speaks at the Monongahela House on his way to Washington.
The Secretary of War orders heavy guns shipped from the Allegheny Arsenal to Southern forts. A mass meeting blocks the shipment, and the order is countermanded.
The Union calls for men and guns. The Fort Pitt Foundry casts great Rodman cannon; every mill runs night and day.
The first firm bearing the Jones and Laughlin name is organized, headquartered at Third and Ross downtown.

Event Name: Dixmont Asylum; West Penn Goes to War
Description: Western Pennsylvania's first mental hospital opens at Dixmont. The Army takes over West Penn Hospital as a military hospital for three years.
An explosion tears through the Allegheny Arsenal's cartridge laboratory in Lawrenceville, killing 78 workers, most of them young women.

Event Name: Defences Thrown Up on the Hills
Description: As Lee's army invades Pennsylvania, thousands of workers dig earthworks on the hills around the city. The rebels turn back at Gettysburg.

Event Name: Iron Wages Tied to Iron Prices
Description: Ending an eight-month strike, ironmasters sign the Vulcans' first contract: a sliding scale linking puddlers' pay to the price of bar iron.
Peace returns. War contracts end, but railroads and cities across the country need iron as never before.
The state lets railroads commission private police. A year later the power extends to coal and iron companies, at $1 per commission.
The Allegheny Observatory passes to Western University. Samuel Langley becomes director two years later.
Allegheny City turns its old common pasture into a landscaped public park.
Failed strikes break 11 Sons of Vulcan locals this year and 16 more the next.
A visiting writer describes the smoky valley at night as 'hell with the lid off'. The name sticks.

Event Name: The City Annexes the East End
Description: Pittsburgh annexes Lawrenceville, Oakland, East Liberty and the farms beyond, tripling its area.
Young George Westinghouse receives his patent for a railroad air brake.
Henry J. Heinz and L.C. Noble form Heinz, Noble & Company in Sharpsburg to sell bottled horseradish.
The Westinghouse Air Brake Company is incorporated and starts production in Pittsburgh the next year.
A college for women, the future Chatham, is founded in Pittsburgh.
The first passenger incline lifts workers up Coal Hill to the new streets of Mt. Washington.
The Fifteenth Amendment is ratified. Black Pennsylvanians, disfranchised since 1838, can vote again.
Westinghouse Air Brake becomes one of the first American firms to give workers a Saturday half-day.
Henry Clay Frick, 21, joins two cousins and a friend to turn Connellsville coal into coke.

Event Name: The South Side Joins the City
Description: Birmingham and the other South Side boroughs are annexed to Pittsburgh.
Carnegie breaks ground for a Bessemer steel works at Braddock's Field, named for the Pennsylvania Railroad's president.
The Flagler brothers of Boston open a pipe works at McKeesport. It becomes the fastest-growing town in the nation.
The collapse of Jay Cooke's bank starts the Long Depression. Orders vanish; wages are cut across the valley.
Andrew Carnegie's Edgar Thomson Works at Braddock rolls its first Bessemer steel rail. A new age of steel begins.
The Long Depression sinks young H.J. Heinz's business. He restarts as F & J Heinz and adds ketchup.
At Emerald Hall, Pittsburgh, the Vulcans, Heaters and Roll Hands merge into the Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers.
Samuel Diescher's incline begins hauling riders up Mount Washington at a grade of up to 30 degrees.
Railroad workers strike against wage cuts. Militia fire on a crowd at 28th Street; the crowd burns the Pennsylvania Railroad's roundhouse and hundreds of cars.
Catholic Holy Ghost Fathers found the college that becomes Duquesne University.
Last rails are laid to Youngstown. The P&LE is the only major line free of the Pennsylvania Railroad and is an immediate success.
Slovak, Hungarian, Polish and Rusyn labourers begin arriving for mill jobs, recruited by agents and letters home.
With loans from the Mellon bank, Frick buys out his partners and forms H.C. Frick & Company.
The Allegheny County Light Company is founded with $90,000 to sell electric light.
Republican Christopher Magee runs the votes while contractor William Flinn takes the paving and sewer contracts. Their machine will rule the city for two decades.
The Pittsburgh Bessemer Steel Company opens a works on the Homestead flats. Carnegie buys it two years later.
Westinghouse Air Brake moves to a bigger plant in Allegheny City. Within ten years it builds a company town at Wilmerding.
Westinghouse founds Union Switch & Signal at Swissvale to build railroad signals.
The Coke King meets Andrew Carnegie in New York. Their partnership forms the next year, joining coke to steel.
After the courthouse burns, Western University sells its downtown buildings to Allegheny County and moves out.
Father Mollinger completes St. Anthony's Chapel on Troy Hill, with thousands of relics. Pilgrims arrive by the trainload.
Gustav Lindenthal's lenticular truss bridge replaces Roebling's suspension span over the Monongahela.
John B. Ford and John Pitcairn found Pittsburgh Plate Glass, with its first works at Creighton on the Allegheny.
Anarchists meet in Pittsburgh, found the International Working People's Association, and reject reform through the ballot.
The rivers rise high in February, flooding wharves and riverfront mills.
Natural gas is piped into Pittsburgh's mills and homes. For a few years the smoke thins and the sky turns blue.
Blast furnaces rise at Rankin across the river from Homestead.
Shadyside Hospital opens a school of nursing.
The first dam on the Ohio River opens at Avalon. The great wicket dam gives the harbor deep water in all seasons.
George Westinghouse founds his electric company to sell alternating current. The battle of the currents begins.
Open-hearth furnaces are installed at the Homestead Works.
After three decades of iron, J&L begins making steel.
A general hospital opens in Allegheny City.
A new charter centralizes city government in departments such as Public Works and Public Safety, which the ring uses to steer contracts.
Alfred Hunt and Charles Martin Hall open an experimental aluminum smelter on Smallman Street.
H. H. Richardson's massive stone courthouse and jail open on Grant's Hill.
On Thanksgiving Day the Smallman Street works pours the first commercial aluminum. The metal sells for nearly $5 a pound.
Heinz gains control of the family firm and renames it the H.J. Heinz Company.
The South Fork Dam, owned by a club of Pittsburgh industrialists, fails upriver. More than 2,200 die in Johnstown; relief trains leave from Pittsburgh.
Carnegie personally dedicates the first Carnegie library in America near his Edgar Thomson Works. A basement bathhouse lets millworkers wash before reading.
Public Works chief Edward Bigelow spends over $900,000 buying farms parcel by parcel for a 377-acre park around the city reservoirs.

Event Name: Schenley Park Given to the City
Description: Mary Schenley gives 300 acres of land in Oakland for a great public park.
The Carnegie Free Library of Allegheny opens. It was the first library Andrew Carnegie commissioned, though Braddock's opened first.
The Second Avenue Traction Company runs electric streetcars. Horsecars begin to vanish.
Congress raises import duties to about 50%, with new protection for tinplate. Pittsburgh steel and glass men cheer, and tinplate mills rise along the Mon.
Striking coke workers march on Frick's company store at Morewood. National Guardsmen fire into the crowd of a thousand, killing nine.
Pittsburgh Reduction begins smelting at New Kensington, the start of an aluminum town on the Allegheny.
Brothers Frank and Ralph Dravo found a contracting firm in Pittsburgh.
Westinghouse installs the nation's first alternating-current power system, at a Colorado mine.
Heinz coins his famous "57 Varieties" slogan.
The Western Pennsylvania Medical College merges into Western University.
Locked-out steelworkers fight Pinkerton guards landing from barges at the Homestead Works. Seven workers and three Pinkertons die; the state militia occupies the town and the union is broken.
Anarchist Alexander Berkman shoots and stabs Henry Clay Frick in his office downtown. Frick survives and returns to work within a week.
On July 1, Carnegie consolidates all his plants into the Carnegie Steel Company, days before the Homestead lockout.
West Penn Hospital opens a nursing school with 15 students.
Nearly bankrupt, the Amalgamated Association votes on November 20 to send its men back to Homestead.
Company and union drop their criminal charges against each other, closing the Homestead affair in the courts.
Stung by the Homestead barges, Congress bars the federal government from hiring Pinkerton agents or similar private armies.
Westinghouse alternating current lights the Chicago World's Fair, and the company wins the Niagara Falls generator contract.
Banks and railroads fail across the country. Mills close; soup kitchens open in the mill towns.
Highland Park opens to the public four years after the city began buying land.
An addition gives the Braddock library a 964-seat music hall, gymnasium, swimming pool and bowling alleys. Carnegie employees pay half price.
Henry Phipps gives the city a great glasshouse in Schenley Park and insists it open on Sundays so working people can visit.
The United Mine Workers call a national bituminous coal strike, and pits across the Pittsburgh district go idle.
Allegheny City's mayor and residents pool money to buy the Watson farm for a 251-acre park crowned by the Allegheny Observatory.
Six Croatian benefit societies merge in Allegheny City into a national federation headquartered in Pittsburgh.
Banker Andrew Mellon, whose father graduated in 1837, joins Western University's board of trustees.
Westinghouse generators at Niagara's Adams plant send power about 20 miles to Buffalo.
Carnegie's library, music hall and museum open in Oakland.
The Pittsburgh Orchestra is founded and plays in Carnegie Music Hall.
Streetcar magnate Christopher Magee offers the city a zoo, provided it sits in Highland Park at the end of his trolley line.
Carnegie's Union Railroad links his works along the Monongahela, moving hot metal and ore between mills.
Westinghouse and General Electric pool their electrical patents, ending the war of the currents in court.
Frick crushes an attempt to rebuild the union at Homestead. Carnegie also beats union drives at Duquesne and Edgar Thomson.
Jones & Laughlin refuses to sign with the Amalgamated Association, starting the de-unionization of Pittsburgh's mills.
The federal government seizes the private Monongahela Navigation Company's locks and dams by eminent domain. Tolls on coal barges end.
The Carnegie Library's first branch opens, the first in America with open shelves and a children's room.
Ten thousand people, many riding Magee's trolleys, attend the zoo's dedication.
George Mesta merges two machine shops into a heavy-machinery maker at West Homestead.
Carnegie adds the Rankin blast furnaces across the river to his Homestead empire.

Event Name: Homestead Library Opens Above the Mill
Description: Carnegie's $300,000 library, music hall and athletic club opens on the hill overlooking the works where the 1892 strike was fought.
Sisters Margaret and Stella Stein become Western University's first women graduates.
Andrew Mellon's Monongahela Street Railway buys the Kenny family's picnic grove to draw riders to the end of the line.
The West End branch opens with open stacks.
State Republican boss Matthew Quay of Beaver is acquitted of misusing state funds. A deadlocked legislature leaves his Senate seat empty for two years.
Three hundred Homestead men secretly form a union lodge. Frick shuts the works down.
Mellon's trolley park opens above the Monongahela, drawing three times the zoo's opening crowd.
Carnegie's fossil hunters find a giant dinosaur skeleton near Medicine Bow. It is named Diplodocus carnegii.
National Tube merges with 20 pipe makers into the National Tube Company, soon the world's largest steel-pipe producer.
Dozens of river and rail mines combine into the Pittsburgh Coal Company.
Carnegie Steel posts a record net profit of $21 million for the year.
No unionized steel plant remains in Pennsylvania. Amalgamated membership has fallen from 24,000 to about 8,000 in a decade.
With ten plants, Pittsburgh Plate Glass controls 65% of the nation's plate glass and is its second-largest paint maker.
J.P. Morgan's interests merge bridge builders into the American Bridge Company, headquartered in Pittsburgh.
Andrew Carnegie founds a technical school in Oakland to train the sons and daughters of working families.
Oil gushes at Spindletop, Texas. The Mellons are the largest investors in the venture that becomes Gulf Oil.
J. P. Morgan buys Carnegie Steel for $480 million and forms the United States Steel Corporation, the first billion-dollar company. Dozens of Pittsburgh men become millionaires overnight.
Boss Magee dies. The Quay legislature abolishes the elected mayor and lets the governor appoint a "recorder" to run the city.
Philander Knox, Carnegie Steel's lawyer through Homestead and the U.S. Steel merger, becomes Attorney General.
U.S. Steel offers to recognize the union at most sheet mills. AA president Shaffer demands all plants, and Morgan withdraws the offer.
Thousands of strikebreakers and no help from the AFL break the strike. The union loses most of its U.S. Steel lodges.
The traction companies combine into Pittsburgh Railways, a 400-mile streetcar monopoly.
Phipps gives $30,000 for a teaching hall where schoolchildren take botany classes.
Lincoln Steffens's magazine exposé lays bare the Magee–Flinn machine to the whole nation.
Most of Pittsburgh's electric companies are consolidated into Duquesne Light.
The Pittsburgh Pirates play Boston in the first modern World Series. Boston wins.
U.S. Steel buys a half-interest in Crucible Steel's furnaces and steel plant at Clairton.
An explosion at Cheswick kills 179 miners and two rescuers. One boy survives. A third of Homestead's Hungarian Reformed congregation is lost.
Moved by the Harwick rescuers' deaths, Carnegie endows a $5 million fund to honor civilians who risk their lives for others.
George Gould opens an $800,000 Beaux-Arts terminal and a tunnel through Mount Washington to break the Pennsylvania Railroad's grip.
A plaster cast of Carnegie's dinosaur is unveiled in London, the first of many given to the world's museums.
Jones & Laughlin begins a vast new works and company town at Aliquippa on the Ohio.
American Bridge incorporates a company town on the old Harmony Society lands. It will grow from 5,000 to 20,000 people in twenty years.
Reformer George Guthrie wins the mayoralty on a fusion ticket against the Republican organization.
Westinghouse sets up a formal research and development department.
Pittsburgh Reduction renames itself the Aluminum Company of America. Mellon's brother Richard is president.
Mellon oil interests, including Guffey Petroleum, combine into the Gulf Oil Corporation.
The rivers rise to 36 feet. Downtown streets and the riverfront mills are under water for days.
The original Diplodocus skeleton goes on display in the enlarged Carnegie Institute.
Two new blast furnaces fire up at Rankin. They will run for seventy years.
More than half the union's iron puddlers break away under the old Sons of Vulcan name.
A run on the banks spreads from New York. Orders are cancelled and furnaces banked.
In the panic, Westinghouse Electric's board forces George Westinghouse to take leave. Bankers take control, though he keeps the air brake company.
After a long legal fight, the city of Allegheny is annexed to Pittsburgh and becomes the North Side.
An explosion near Van Meter kills 239 men and boys, the worst coal-mine disaster in Pennsylvania history. Most are Rusyn, Hungarian and Slovak immigrants.
Western University buys a 43-acre site in Oakland for a new campus.
Social investigators document twelve-hour shifts, seven-day weeks, industrial deaths and typhoid in the mill districts.
The legislature renames Western University the University of Pittsburgh.
Gould's Wabash venture into Pittsburgh collapses financially.
An explosion kills 154 men in the Pittsburgh Buffalo Company's "model" mine town. One survives.
The city's sand filtration plant opens. Typhoid deaths, once the worst in the nation, fall sharply.
Immigrant workers at McKees Rocks strike against the 'pool' pay system. State troopers and strikebreakers clash with strikers; a dozen die.
The Pirates open their steel-and-concrete ballpark in Oakland.
U.S. Steel withdraws recognition at its last 12 union mills. The tin-plate workers strike.
Honus Wagner and the Pirates beat Ty Cobb's Detroit Tigers.
University departments move to Oakland under Hornbostel's "Acropolis" plan. Only four of its buildings are ever built.
Miners strike across Westmoreland County. Before it ends in July 1911, deputies and state police have killed six miners.
Deputies and state police fire into a crowd of striking miners at Yukon, killing one.
Prosecutors reveal that bankers bribed city councilmen to win city deposits. Dozens of councilmen are indicted or confess.
The Pittsburgh Courier is incorporated. It grows into one of the nation's leading Black newspapers.
Unable to meet $14 million in debts, George Westinghouse is pushed out of his electric company. He cuts all ties the next year.
After 14 months, the union's strike against U.S. Steel collapses. Big Steel is union-free.
The state replaces the city's two ward-based councils with a nine-member council elected at large, and replaces ward school boards with a judge-appointed board.
West Penn Hospital moves into a new building in Bloomfield.
Under Cumberland Posey, a team of Black mill workers takes the name Homestead Grays.
Downtown's Grant's Hill is lowered by fourteen feet to level the streets around the courthouse.
The Carnegie Technical Schools become the Carnegie Institute of Technology, granting four-year degrees.
With ex-boss William Flinn among his leaders, Theodore Roosevelt's Progressives carry Pennsylvania.
Andrew and Richard Mellon found an institute of industrial research, at first a department of Pitt.
War breaks out in Europe. Immigration stops almost overnight while orders for steel and shells pour in.
A zinc smelter starts up at Donora beside the American Steel & Wire works.
Duquesne Light begins what may be the world's first 69,000-volt urban power ring.
Pennsylvania's men reject a women's suffrage amendment by about 55,000 votes despite a hard campaign by Pittsburgh suffragists.
Black families from the South arrive for mill jobs left open by the war, settling in the Hill District, Homestead and Beltzhoover.
About 3,100 motormen and conductors walk out for three days. They win raises, and crowds cheer the first trolley back on Fifth Avenue.
Striking Westinghouse workers march on the Edgar Thomson gate, and guards open fire, killing three. The National Guard arrives and the strike breaks.
U.S. Steel opens an $18 million plant with 1,500 by-product coke ovens that capture coal tar and benzol.
The city opens Schenley High School in Oakland, a showpiece of Progressive-era school building.
The United States declares war on Germany. The mills run at full capacity; German street names are changed.
Westinghouse Air Brake acquires Union Switch & Signal.
War orders lift Alcoa's output 40%. New Kensington employs 3,292 by war's end.
The influenza pandemic hits Pittsburgh harder than almost any American city. Schools, churches and saloons close.
The war ends on November 11. Steel orders fall away.
Dravo starts a shipyard on Neville Island in the Ohio.
Four years after its voters said no, Pennsylvania ratifies the women's suffrage amendment.
Coal company guards shoot organizer Fannie Sellins and miner Joseph Starzeleski outside a Brackenridge mine. A jury later acquits.
Some 350,000 steelworkers walk out nationwide demanding union recognition and the eight-hour day. Strikers are arrested and meetings banned; the strike collapses by January.
Mother Jones is arrested for speaking to strikers. Asked who gave her permission, she names Patrick Henry, Jefferson and Adams.
The saloons close. Speakeasies open in back rooms in every neighbourhood.
H.C. Frick dies and leaves the city land and money for a large park in the East End.
Westinghouse's KDKA in East Pittsburgh makes the first commercial radio broadcast, reporting the Harding-Cox election returns.
Congress passes emergency immigration quotas. The great waves from Southern and Eastern Europe come to an end.
Pittsburgh banker Andrew Mellon becomes Treasury Secretary. He will serve three presidents.
A business school is founded that becomes Robert Morris University.
The United Mine Workers strike nationwide. Pittsburgh-district mines stay shut into the summer.
The old Davis Island dam is retired and a new dam at Emsworth takes over.
Under public pressure, U.S. Steel ends the twelve-hour shift.
The $6 million twin tunnels through Mount Washington open the South Hills to commuters and suburbs.
Permanent quotas all but close immigration from Southern and Eastern Europe. The mill towns' ethnic neighbourhoods stop growing from abroad.
U.S. Steel centralizes coke making at Clairton. Patch-town mines and beehive ovens close across the coalfields.
The University of Pittsburgh opens a large football stadium in Oakland.
The Revenue Act of 1926 completes Mellon's program, cutting the top income-tax rate to 25% and slashing estate taxes.
The University of Pittsburgh starts building its 42-storey Gothic skyscraper in Oakland.
Commissioner E.V. Babcock buys land at his own cost for North Park, over 3,000 acres. South Park opens too, home of the county fair.
A Rapp & Rapp movie palace opens on Sixth Street.
Repair work on the world's largest gas tank sets off a blast on the North Side. Twenty-eight die and buildings for half a mile are wrecked.
A new Monongahela bridge links downtown directly to the Liberty Tubes.
Three matching self-anchored suspension bridges open over the Allegheny at Sixth, Seventh and Ninth Streets.
Coal and Iron Police beat miner John Barkoski at Imperial. He dies the next morning, and a jury acquits three officers.
Legislator Michael Musmanno campaigns to abolish the private police. A weakened reform, the Mustin Act, passes.
A charter to federate the city and county boroughs wins a countywide majority but fails the two-thirds rule in most towns.
The stock market collapses. By 1932 the mills run at a fifth of capacity.
The last locks are finished, and the Ohio becomes a chain of slackwater pools from Pittsburgh to Cairo.
The Sisters of Mercy found Mount Mercy College, later Carlow.
Governor Gifford Pinchot refuses to issue or renew Coal and Iron Police commissions, effectively ending the system.
Mercy Hospital gives more than $600,000 in free care to the Depression's jobless.
Allegheny County Airport opens in West Mifflin, the third-largest airport in the nation.
Father James Cox of Old St. Patrick's leads 25,000 unemployed Pittsburghers to Washington to demand relief.
Congressman Wright Patman files impeachment charges against Mellon. Hoover sends him to London as ambassador and the charges lapse.
Numbers king Gus Greenlee opens a $100,000 ballpark in the Hill District, home of the Crawfords and the Grays.
Campaigning at Forbes Field, Franklin Roosevelt attacks Hoover's deficits and promises a balanced budget.
The National Industrial Recovery Act promises workers the right to organize. Organizers flood into the mill towns.
Half of Clairton's workers join a round-the-clock strike. The miners win a contract, but the steelworkers do not.
More than 6,000 J&L workers at Aliquippa sign union cards. At Duquesne a quarter of the unskilled men join.
Deputies recruited with J&L's help attack strikers at the Spang-Chalfant tube mill in Ambridge, killing one.
Miners strike the coal mines owned by the steel companies. President Roosevelt intervenes publicly.
With David Lawrence's party behind him, William McNair becomes the first Democratic mayor in decades.
Prohibition ends. The saloons and clubs reopen legally.
Mesta wins the contract to equip U.S. Steel's new continuous strip mill at Irvin.
Days before a planned national steel strike, AFL chief William Green persuades the union to cancel it.
George Earle is elected governor, and Pittsburgh's Joseph Guffey wins a Senate seat. Lawrence joins the state cabinet.
Penn State opens a campus in the mill town of McKeesport.
The Supreme Court kills the NIRA in May. In July, Congress passes the Wagner Act, guaranteeing collective bargaining.
The Earle administration formally ends the private industrial police.
John L. Lewis forms the Committee for Industrial Organization inside the AFL to organize mass-production workers.
The worst flood in the city's history crests at 46 feet. Downtown is under water to the second floor, the mills stand idle and power fails for days.
Philip Murray's SWOC opens offices in the mill towns and signs up workers in secret.
Three months after the great flood, Congress authorizes a reservoir system for the upper Ohio, Allegheny and Monongahela.
Feuding with Lawrence over WPA patronage, Mayor McNair resigns. Lawrence ally Cornelius Scully takes over.
U.S. Steel recognises the union without a strike. Two months later Jones & Laughlin's men strike and win too.
In NLRB v. Jones & Laughlin, the Supreme Court upholds the Wagner Act 5–4 and orders fired Aliquippa organizers reinstated.

Event Name: Death on the Beaver Falls Picket
Description: A deputy's tear-gas shell fatally wounds a striker on a steel picket line at Beaver Falls.
Earle's legislature passes a state labor relations act, wage and hour laws, and creates the Turnpike Commission.
The city creates a housing authority under the new federal Housing Act to build public homes for working families.
The Mellon Institute's colonnaded research building is completed on Fifth Avenue.
Frank Lloyd Wright completes Fallingwater, a country house for the Kaufmann department-store family, in the Laurel Highlands.
The Justice Department charges Alcoa with monopolizing aluminum and seeks to break it up.
The first of the Pittsburgh District's flood-control dams is finished on a Monongahela tributary in West Virginia.
The Heinz family dedicates a Gothic chapel at Pitt in memory of H.J. Heinz and his mother.
War breaks out in Europe. Orders for steel climb.
The Buhl Foundation opens a $1 million planetarium and science museum on the North Side.
Democratic boss David Lawrence is tried on graft charges from the Earle years and acquitted.
"America's First Superhighway" opens from Irwin to Carlisle, reusing tunnels from an abandoned railroad.
FDR dedicates Terrace Village in the Hill District, one of the nation's largest public housing projects.
City council passes a smoke-control law. War delays enforcement for five years.
America enters the war. The valley becomes the arsenal of democracy; Dravo builds landing ships on Neville Island.
The Pittsburgh Courier launches its "Double V" campaign: victory over fascism abroad and over racism at home.
SWOC becomes the United Steelworkers of America.
Dravo becomes the first company to receive the Army-Navy "E" Award. Its Neville Island yard will employ 16,000.
Business and civic leaders under Richard King Mellon form a council to clean up the smoke and rebuild downtown.
West Homestead forges 16-inch naval guns, propeller shafts and "Long Tom" cannon and wins a six-star Army-Navy "E".
The war ends. Workers and veterans want higher wages and better homes.
Party boss David Lawrence wins the mayoralty and allies with Richard King Mellon's Republican business elite.
Three-quarters of a million steelworkers strike nationwide for higher wages.
About 75,000 Westinghouse workers, led by the UE, strike for 115 days and win an 18.5-cent raise.
About 250 mounted and foot state troopers break up a crowd of 2,000 Westinghouse strikers at the plant gates.
The city's smoke ordinance takes effect for homes and mills. Coal gives way to natural gas and the skies begin to clear.
Power workers strike Duquesne Light, threatening to black out the region's homes and mills.
The city forms the URA with Mayor Lawrence as chairman. Its first project is Gateway Center at the Point.
Harrisburg passes a bundle of Pittsburgh laws: county smoke control, a parking authority, a sanitary authority and broad local taxing power.
Congress passes the Taft-Hartley Act over Truman's veto. Pittsburgh's unions split into factions.
Duquesne Light announces a $28 million coal-fired power station at Elrama.
A temperature inversion traps smoke from the zinc works in Donora, up the Monongahela. Twenty die; thousands fall ill.
WDTV signs on as Pittsburgh's first television station.
The CIO expels the left-led electrical workers' union. Westinghouse locals split, and Monsignor Charles Owen Rice leads the anti-communist side.
Steelworkers strike for company-paid pensions and win them.
Homer S. Brown, author of the state's 1935 equal-rights law, becomes the first Black judge on the county Common Pleas court.
The old warehouse district at the Point is cleared for Gateway Center and Point State Park.
The census counts 676,806 Pittsburghers, the most the city will ever have.
FBI informant Matt Cvetic names local unionists as communists. Their lawyer, Hymen Schlesinger, is himself put on trial.
President Truman seizes the steel industry to prevent a wartime strike. The Supreme Court overturns the seizure and the men walk out.
A new airport opens in Moon Township, served by five airlines.
Mesta builds a 50,000-ton forging press for the Air Force, run by Alcoa to shape aircraft parts.
A flood-control dam near Saltsburg is finished to guard the Kiskiminetas and Allegheny valleys.
The first section of the Parkway East opens through an $18 million tunnel, the costliest state road project yet.
WQED becomes the nation's first community-sponsored television station.
The Turnpike's Western Extension is completed past Pittsburgh to the Ohio line.
After trials with 1.8 million schoolchildren, Jonas Salk's Pitt polio vaccine is declared "safe, effective, and potent."
Electrical workers begin a five-month strike against Westinghouse.
Bulldozers clear the Lower Hill District for a civic arena, displacing 8,000 residents and hundreds of businesses.
The legislature creates the Port Authority of Allegheny County. It will later take over the region's transit.
Steelworkers strike nationwide for a month in July.
The first full-scale nuclear power plant in America begins sending power to Pittsburgh.
The county plans a ring of new regional parks: Boyce, Round Hill, Settlers Cabin, Deer Lakes, Harrison Hills and White Oak.
Mayor Lawrence is elected the state's first Catholic governor. His deputy Joseph Barr becomes mayor.
After a record $100 million loan, the county's new treatment plant ends the routine dumping of raw sewage into the rivers.
The longest steel strike in history. Customers turn to imported steel and many never come back.
A double-deck bridge carries the new freeway from the Point across the Monongahela.
Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev tours the Mesta machine works at West Homestead.
Bill Mazeroski's ninth-inning home run wins the World Series for the Pirates over the Yankees.
The $16 million tunnel completes a direct freeway from the airport and the West into downtown.
A new college opens downtown.
Following the AFL–CIO merger, local unions form the Allegheny County Labor Council.
The domed arena with its retractable stainless-steel roof opens in the cleared Lower Hill.
U.S. Steel fires a giant new blast furnace, "Dorothy Six," at the Duquesne Works.
La Roche College is founded and Pitt opens a Greensburg campus.
The Port Authority buys out Pittsburgh Railways and 32 bus and incline companies, creating a single public transit system.
Westinghouse posts record sales of $2.1 billion.
Chancellor Edward Litchfield leaves amid a financial crisis that threatens the university.
A 179-foot dam tames the upper Allegheny. Its reservoir floods Seneca Nation land, and the Seneca call it "Lake Perfidy."
The Commonwealth rescues Pitt, bringing public money and lower tuition for Pennsylvanians.
The Community College of Allegheny County opens to train and retrain the region's workers.
The Pittsburgh Courier, once read by 357,000, prints its last issue. It is relaunched as the New Pittsburgh Courier.
Carnegie Tech merges with the Mellon Institute to form Carnegie Mellon University.
Long a union holdout, the Mesta works votes in a union.
Fred Rogers's program debuts nationally from WQED.
After the murder of Martin Luther King, Jr., unrest breaks out in the Hill District and Homewood.
Dallas conglomerate Ling-Temco-Vought buys 63% of J&L for about $428 million. Control of a Pittsburgh giant moves to Texas.
The first new regional park opens in Monroeville and Plum, with the county's only ski slope.
American Standard buys Westinghouse Air Brake.
A job-training center opens on the North Side.
Pittsburgh Plate Glass renames itself PPG Industries.
Mary Flinn Lawrence offers her 629-acre estate and mansion to the county.
Nate Smith's Black Construction Coalition shuts down public building sites, including Three Rivers Stadium, demanding jobs in the all-white trades.
Councilman Pete Flaherty beats the Democratic machine's candidate and wins the mayoralty, promising to cut patronage.
The Pirates and Steelers move to a new stadium on the North Side.
West Penn's Mellon Pavilion opens with a burn care unit serving the mill district.
Roberto Clemente leads the Pirates to a World Series title.
Heinz money turns the shuttered Loew's Penn into a $10 million home for the Pittsburgh Symphony.
The wettest storm in Pennsylvania's history drives 100,000 from their homes. The Allegheny rises seven inches an hour.
Steel mills stop dumping slag in the Nine Mile Run valley.
U.S. Steel and the county agree to clean Clairton's air within ten years. An EPA official calls the plant "Dante's Inferno."
Franco Harris's last-second catch gives the Steelers their first playoff win.
The state and county sue U.S. Steel over 241 air-pollution violations at Clairton.
The steelworkers and ten steelmakers sign the Experimental Negotiating Agreement, trading national strikes for 3% yearly raises, cost-of-living pay and arbitration.
The Arab oil embargo sends energy prices soaring. Detroit's car sales, and its steel orders, fall.
The fountain at the Point is turned on, completing the park where Fort Pitt stood.
After 85 years, the Braddock Carnegie Library closes. The declining mill town cannot fix its roof.
U.S. Steel announces a $100 million cleanup at Clairton. The state environment secretary calls the plant a national disgrace.
The Steelers win their first Super Bowl.
Gulf Oil's chairman and other executives are forced out over illegal political contributions.
A regional air-pollution emergency centers on Clairton. The EPA links it to 14 deaths, and U.S. Steel warns it cannot make steel without the coke.
Soaring uranium prices break Westinghouse's fixed-price fuel contracts. Lawsuits will cost it $950 million.
Volkswagen chooses New Stanton for its American plant with a $40 million state loan. It will employ over 6,000.
Beaver Valley Unit 1 is commissioned at Shippingport.
Hill District legislator K. Leroy Irvis becomes the first Black speaker of any state legislature since Reconstruction.
Flaherty leaves for the Justice Department. Council president Richard Caliguiri becomes mayor and wins election as an independent.
One of the nation's first bus-only roads opens to the South Hills.

Event Name: J&L Cuts Back in the City
Description: Jones & Laughlin announces closures at its Pittsburgh works, one of the first big shutdowns in the city.
Mayor Caliguiri announces a second downtown building boom of new office towers.
Rankin's last blast furnaces shut down after seventy years.
LTV's Jones & Laughlin absorbs Youngstown Sheet & Tube.
The Pirates win the World Series and the Steelers will win a fourth Super Bowl in January.
U.S. Steel announces the shutdown of plants across the country. Imports, old open hearths and lost markets catch up with the valley.
The census counts 423,938 people, down more than a third from the 1950 peak.
Steel demand collapses in a deep recession. Layoffs spread through every mill town.
U.S. Steel shuts major operations at McKeesport's tube works, laying off 2,400 of 4,800.
Dravo closes its Neville Island shipyard.
Westinghouse acquires robot maker Unimation.
Carnegie Mellon begins building a campus-wide computer network. Its research budget has grown nearly tenfold.
Nearly one in five workers in the Monongahela Valley is out of work. Food banks open in union halls.
Mesta Machine files for bankruptcy. Most of the West Homestead works is sold by summer.
The 6.8-mile Martin Luther King Jr. East Busway opens to Wilkinsburg.
American Bridge ends operations in the town it built.
Residents buy the doomed Braddock library for $1 and reopen a children's library.
U.S. Steel shuts the Duquesne Works. A campaign to save its giant 'Dorothy Six' blast furnace fails.
Fending off raider T. Boone Pickens, Gulf accepts Chevron's $13.2 billion offer, the largest merger in history.
Washington approves the merger of J&L and Republic. The new LTV Steel ranks second in the nation, and the J&L name disappears.
Modern light-rail cars begin running from South Hills Village through a new Mount Lebanon tunnel.
Employees buy the Weirton steel works, creating the nation's largest employee-owned manufacturer, in exchange for a six-year wage freeze.
Radical clergy and jobless steelworkers disrupt a church Christmas party with skunk-oil balloons to shame U.S. Steel's chairman.
Rev. D. Douglas Roth holds out in his Clairton church, is jailed, and is later defrocked.
Frozen pipes at Clairton spill benzene into the Monongahela at 100 times the legal limit.
Gulf ceases to exist. About 1,500 research and headquarters jobs, a $54 million payroll, leave Pittsburgh.
Clergy and union activists protest plant closings at Shadyside Presbyterian Church.
Wheeling-Pittsburgh Steel files for bankruptcy.
Carnegie Mellon is among the first six universities to register an Internet domain.
LTV Steel's old Jones & Laughlin works in Pittsburgh and most of the Homestead Works have closed. The steel era is ending; what the valley does next is up to those who remain.
Rev. Daniel Solberg barricades himself in his church. Police force their way in and arrest him.
Clergy and unionists hold an open-air service on the plaza of the U.S. Steel Building.
The downtown light-rail subway opens. Streetcars leave downtown streets and the Smithfield Street Bridge for good.
Clairton furloughs 1,600 more workers. The city nearly goes bankrupt and lays off its police and firefighters.
Seven Mon Valley towns form an authority to seize closing mills by eminent domain.
Record rains flood the Monongahela basin in early November.
